brief_context: Quoted in the article regarding the dangers of partial knowledge.
article_title: Doing One's Energy Homework in the '80s
brief_extract: We believe it is important that people everywhere should start to do their energy homework — and, particularly, that they should acquire at least some bare facts about nuclear power — since the energy issue is likely to be predominant in the '80s. "A little learning", wrote Alexander Pope, "is a dangerous thing" — but in our experience none at all is a great deal worse. The EAW will be offering this modest 'fact-kit' in the hope that it may help many to derive more sense from the 'nuclear debate' and to follow or actually participate in it with greater confidence.

A Practical Person
An engineer is by nature a very practical person, dealing with natural materials and forces. Dr Laverick therefore always found it satisfying to work on projects which would fulfil specific needs, and then see those products manufactured as commercially viable items or used for other worth-while purposes. Her total absorption and delight in all aspects of her work is very obvious.

brief_context: Mentioned regarding her family ties and home life.
brief_extract:
One of her projects involves the Code of Ethics for engineers, which provides them with the very necessary guidelines they so often need, particularly when involved in commercial work. Close Family Ties
Elizabeth Laverick has very close family ties, and since her father died recently she has spent a great deal of her spare time visiting her mother who is in failing health. Because of her busy and long working days - her job involves many evening meetings and functions - she has a small flat near her Savoy Place office, spending her weekends between her house in Hertfordshire and her mother's place some 15 miles away in Buckinghamshire.

Some points to be observed if you wish to make the most of cut flowers:
Always use vases with reasonably wide openings so as to avoid a cramped arrangement; floral foam or crumpled chicken wire is useful to hold the stems and prevent the blooms falling over; place your flowers, wrapped in paper, in about six inches of water and leave for 1-2 hours; do not put daffodils or narcissi in the same water with other flowers; daffodils and narcissi should be placed in water and left for at least a day before including them in an arrangement with other flowers, although this precaution can be avoided if floral foam is used to hold the flowers in place in the arrangement; cut stems to different lengths so that every flower can be seen and has adequate 'breathing space'; the best arrangement will make the flowers all seem to come from one point and be as wide as tall; the inclusion of spring foliage such as the stems of birch, prunus or pussy willows will enhance the attractiveness of an arrangement. Then - the automatic
Then in 1955 came another major step forward. In that year Bill Russell and Peter Hobbs, who three years before had founded the now internationally known company of Russell Hobbs to manufacture and market an electric coffee pot, patented and started to market their latest innovation - the automatic electric kettle. They were already marketing kettles of the type conventional at that time, but the unique feature of the new kettle lay in an automatic steam operated switch which disconnected the electric supply as soon as the boiling point of water was reached.

brief_context: Gave an address to the Electrical Women's Round Table.
brief_extract:
The Woman’s Perspective

An address given to the Electrical Women’s Round Table, Cedar Rapids, Iowa, USA on September 24, 1980 by Ann McMullan

I have long looked forward to the day when I might have the pleasure and privilege of attendance at your Conference and I am deeply conscious of the honour you accord, not only to my Association but also to me personally, in inviting me to address you this evening. Historically, this is a very special occasion since our two organisations share so much in common, including a similar lifespan and a number of parallel objectives.

associated_organisation: Women's Engineering Society; Electrical Association for Women (EAW)
brief_context: First Director and Secretary of the EAW.
brief_extract:
The EAW was founded in 1924 by a group of Women's Engineering Society members who were far-sighted enough to realise that there would be a need for electrical education, information and advice since electricity was at that time being introduced rapidly into increasing numbers of households in which the users were predominantly female. The Women's Engineering Society had been formed only 5 years previously and its Secretary, Caroline Haslett became the first Director and Secretary of the EAW. original aims

The original title of the new body was the Women's Electrical Association but this was changed a year later because the initials WEA had already been adopted by the Workers Education Association.

title: Dame
associated_organisation: Electrical Association for Women (EAW); Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust; British Electricity Authority; British Electrical Development Association
brief_context: The first Director of the EAW and industry pioneer.
brief_extract: So much for the background, which may help to put my further remarks into perspective. At this point it is appropriate to pay tribute to the vision and the dynamic influence of our first Director, Dame Caroline Haslett, as she became in 1947. Born in 1895, she grew up with what was then a rare conception of women's capacities, and her own example challenged and inspired women in many other parts of the world.
